newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Clinton rests before talks in Philippines.
newsitem.headline: Clinton rests before talks in Philippines.

text.p: U.S. President Bill Clinton played golf on Saturday in his final moments of relaxation before heading to Manila for an economic summit and talks with the leaders of China, Japan and South Korea.

Taking advantage of sunny skies and Port Douglas' tropical beauty, Clinton took to the fairways early in the morning after he and his wife Hillary took a leisurely sunrise stroll along a strip of beach on the Coral Sea.
The quiet moments were the last for Clinton, who later in the day was to depart for the Philippines -- site of the annual meeting of the 18-member Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) forum.

During his five days in Australia, Clinton mixed business with pleasure -- giving an address to members of its Parliament and calling for stricter environmental rules, while also taking lessons from golfer Greg Norman and snorkelling with his wife along the Great Barrier Reef.
During his own hour of snorkelling on Friday, Clinton took pictures with a waterproof camera, viewed the underwater beauty of the coral and marvelled at the size of a giant clam he came across.
He raved to aides later that the experience was "unforgettable" and "magnificent."

The next phase of his 12-day trip, however, is mostly work -- and much of it diplomatically challenging as he tries to convince Chinese President Jiang Zemin to ease trade barriers viewed as protectionist by the outside world. He also plans to raise human rights concerns.

Clinton has used his 12-day trip to the Pacific Rim to stress U.S. interest in the region and Washington's determination to be a key economic and political player in a part of the world often neglected by the United States in the past.
On Sunday, in addition to private talks with the Chinese leader, Clinton plans separate meetings with Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto and South Korean President Kim Young-sam.
Fresh from his November 5 re-election victory, Clinton is determined to press for his vision of relations among the nations of the Asia Pacific, particularly improving relations with Beijing.
Aides said he intends to explore reviving an idea raised in April for four-way talks among the United States, China and North and South Korea on trying to defuse tensions on the Korean Peninsula.
In his talks with China's leader he also plans to stress that the United States has not revived its old Cold War strategy of containment to use against Beijing.

In July, Washington and Canberra signed a defence agreement aimed at bolstering security ties by upgrading joint U.S.- Australia military facilities, the establishment of a small marine base in Australia and boosting joint training.
The move prompted Beijing to accuse Australia of being used by Washington as part of a containment pincer with Japan.

The APEC meeting, which Clinton elevated four years ago from the ministerial level to the head of government, is not expected to produce dramatic breakthroughs, according to senior U.S. officials. "We hope to deal with real nuts and bolts issues," one official said.
